source.title: Locating and Steering Refusal Beyond Attention

page_placements.theme: Cross-model transfer of directions: fails raw between independent models, works after an alignment map

record.tranche_reason: Uses a harmful-minus-benign mean-difference direction and directly removes or amplifies it, reporting refusal-related behavior on additional architectures and models. The intervention is at architecture-specific write sites rather than an all-layer, all-position residual-stream projection.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many detector, attack, gain, and layer-selection results that do not themselves test the direction’s causal role; these are not included unless they report an outcome of applying or removing the refusal direction. Harm-probe AUROCs are included only as evidence about the distinction between harm readout and refusal control.
record.test_reason: Estimates the difference-in-means refusal direction in SSM, recurrent and hybrid models (new settings), ablates it and adds it, and reports attack-success and over-refusal rates against orthogonalized random controls. It also transports the direction across architectures. Interventions are at per-architecture write sites, not an all-layer residual projection.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that refusal is one representation shared across architectures (a rigid rotation carries it, and removing it jailbreaks the target while a random control does far less). What is architecture-specific is the write site where the direction must be estimated, not where it is applied. Their gate only ties a detect-then-refuse baseline, and the defense needs a target that already refuses. They describe the direction as a dominant axis within a broader subspace but do not test that.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-benign mean-difference direction and causal removal/addition, but estimates and intervenes at architecture-specific fresh write sites; much of the addition evaluation uses a detector-triggered gate. It does not test projecting one residual direction out of every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on architecture-specific direction-estimation site, layer selection, gain calibration, attack family, generation length, and whether the target already has learned refusal. Persona roleplay is less responsive or backfires under single-direction steering; the hybrid's Mamba-site result depends on layer and gain choice.

fits_no_version.finding: A transformer-trained harm probe, transported by rigid rotation, detects harm in Falcon-Mamba as well as the target's own probe and tracks it category by category (r=0.99). Similar transport holds into RWKV and Zamba2 (AUROC 1.00).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm-detection probes transfer across architectures under an orthogonal map.

fits_no_version.finding: Persona-roleplay attacks inject a persona direction that is anti-aligned with refusal at SSM and RWKV write sites (cosine -0.30 to -0.49). Combining refusal amplification with persona ablation lowers Falcon-Mamba roleplay attack success to 17.5%, but the fix does not transfer to RWKV or Zamba2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona jailbreaks add a separate direction that a single-direction refusal intervention cannot counter.

fits_no_version.finding: Harm is highly decodable at Δ, B, C and the mixer output, yet freezing Δ leaves refusal unchanged. The detector's discriminative direction reads harm but does not steer refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A readable harm direction need not be the one that controls refusal (readout vs control).

record.code_released: not stated; code, data, and result files are promised publicly upon publication
record.problems: Several causal-transfer results have small or single-seed samples, especially RWKV and Zamba2; the Zamba2 attention-site ablation is not decisive by itself. The authors report judge disagreement, a narrower random-control margin for RWKV, detector wrapper confounds at some sites, and incomplete or attack-specific effects. Capability is only checked when the detector gate does not fire, not under active ablation or steering.
record.rows_left_out: Did not enumerate every gain-sweep point, layer sweep, detector firing rate, wrapper-hardening result, or additional attack-family result. These are extensive in Tables 6-26 and Appendices A.10-A.41; omitted where they duplicate the principal causal result or concern the detector rather than the refusal direction. Included selected separate model, attack, control, and reversal conditions bearing directly on the claim versions.

untested.parts: Capability under active ablation or addition. The all-layer, all-position residual projection. Addition on plain harmless (Alpaca) prompts: the over-refusal test uses XSTest benign-but-spicy prompts.
Attacks are not shown to suppress the refusal direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
Cites cone and multi-direction work and calls its direction 'one dominant axis', but does not test affine, cone or multi-direction refusal geometry.
No test separating a harmfulness representation from the refusal decision.
No cross-lingual or base-to-instruct transfer; only cross-architecture transfer between instruct models.
Training is not varied. The Codestral-Mamba contrast (lightly safety-tuned, no refusal to amplify) is a single uncontrolled model comparison.

missing.what: Native-direction ablation rows for Llama-3.1 (50.5%), Mistral (50.0%) and Falcon3-Mamba (42.0%). The current R9-R12 values are actually these native numbers.
Rotation-transported Falcon-Mamba→Mistral ablation: 92.5% attack success but only 3.0% coherent. The authors exclude it as degenerate.
Amplifying the mapped direction into Falcon-Mamba lowers attack success 97.0%→28.5%/29.5%. The same amplification helps little at a transformer target's residual.
At 256 new tokens the deployed gain loses coherence (10.5% coherent; prefix 17.5%, roleplay 55.0%), and no gain both stays coherent and defends.
Human raters score RWKV transported ablation 60.7% vs random 5.9%, and the Zamba2 attention site 14.3% vs 6.7%.
Falcon3-Mamba gated addition: fictional framing 56.0%→4.5%, roleplay 13.0%→0.0%.

record.verdict_notes: Version links for V4 and V5 are removed: the persona direction is attack-specific, and the probe AUROCs are decodability only. Several rows (R9-R12) record Table 5's Native column as the transferred value. Table 5 uses the ridge map, while Table 4/A.9 use the standardized rotation. V7 is left untested: Codestral-Mamba differs from Falcon-Mamba in developer, task and Mamba generation, not only in safety tuning. The study's results are mostly single-checkpoint for RWKV and Zamba2, with small n and gain-dependent outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the original all-layer, all-position residual-stream projection as specified. Harmless-request refusal is not tested by adding the direction alone as a direct behavioral intervention; the benign-side results use a detector-triggered gate or an always-on intervention. Capability is checked with the gate, not under ablation.
No refusal-removing weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
Attacks are evaluated against detectors and gates, not shown to work by suppressing the refusal direction itself; no training-against-ablation experiment.
Tests a persona-injection setting where an additional persona direction matters, but does not compare affine, cone, or other general refusal geometries.
Tests a distinction between harm detection/readout and the direction that controls refusal, not a general account of how harmfulness judgments are represented.
Tests transfer across architectures and model variants, not across languages or from base to instruct models as a controlled comparison.
Does not vary the safety-training data, timing, or procedure experimentally; it contrasts checkpoints with different stated safety-tuning characteristics.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Refusal-direction removal and write-site amplification on tested safety-tuned models and harmful prompts
reader_labels.reason: Removing native or transferred directions raises attack success, and write-site amplification reduces it substantially in the reported settings (R7-R12, R19, R21, R25-R30).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Completeness, attack type, and target behavior
reader_labels.reason: Ablation leaves many refusals in place, some attack reductions are incomplete, roleplay remains resistant or backfires, and a lightly safety-tuned code model has no refusal to amplify (R7-R12, R19, R28, R31, R33, R34). The reported capability equality is only with an inert detector gate (R37).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Always-on refusal-direction amplification raises benign over-refusal from 12.0% to 86.0%, consistent with induced refusal on harmless inputs (R36).

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: Transported probes track target probes, and transported directions increase attack success over relevant controls across the reported architecture pairs (R5-R23).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: RWKV-6 and Zamba2 attention-site transfer ablations
reader_labels.reason: The RWKV random-direction control itself raises attack success substantially, while the Zamba2 attention-site transported effect is modest and its intervals overlap the random control (R20, R23).
